Sonority means the quality of sound that is rich, full, deep, and resonant — the kind of sound that seems to fill a space and linger in the air rather than just hitting your ears and disappearing.

Think of the deep, warm toll of a large church bell. Or a trained opera singer's voice booming through a concert hall. Or a cello note that seems to vibrate in your chest. That richness, that fullness, that sense of the sound carrying weight and depth — that is sonority.
The Most Important Distinction: Sonority ≠ Loudness

This is crucial, and most learners miss it.

A sound can be loud without sonority — like a sharp clap, a gunshot, or someone banging a tin can. These are loud, but thin and brief. They don't resonate or fill the space.

A sound can have great sonority even at moderate volume — like a double bass playing softly in a quiet room. It still has depth, body, and richness. The sound feels full.

So sonority is not about how loud something is. It's about how rich, round, resonant, and full-bodied the sound is. It's the quality that makes a sound feel substantial rather than thin or sharp or flat.

In everyday language, sonority describes the pleasing, resonant quality of sounds — especially voices and instruments.

  • A radio announcer might be praised for the sonority of his voice — meaning it's deep, smooth, and carries beautifully.
  • A violin made by a master craftsman might be admired for the sonority it produces — rich tones that project powerfully across a room.
  • A poorly built guitar might be criticized for its lack of sonority — it sounds thin and dull.
  • A grand cathedral might be said to give the choir's singing a remarkable sonority — because the stone walls reflect and amplify the sound, adding depth and body.

The word often carries a positive connotation. When you say something has sonority, you're usually complimenting it.

In music, sonority has a broader meaning. It refers not just to the richness of a single instrument or voice, but to the overall sound quality and texture that a musical ensemble produces — the way all the elements blend together into a full, resonant whole.

A conductor might talk about the sonority of the orchestra — meaning the collective, blended sound: how rich and balanced it is, how the instruments complement each other, whether the sound is full and deep or thin and harsh.

Composers think carefully about sonority when writing music. If you place too many instruments in a high register playing at once, you might lose sonority — the result sounds shrill. If you balance the high and low voices well, the music gains sonority — it sounds lush and full.

In this musical sense, sonority is almost like a measure of acoustic beauty and depth — a property of sound that great musicians and composers are always chasing.

This is a completely separate, more technical use of the word — but important to know, because linguists and language learners encounter it often.

In phonetics (the study of speech sounds), sonority refers to the relative loudness or acoustic openness of a speech sound — how much sound energy a particular sound carries compared to others.

Here is the key idea: not all sounds you make with your mouth are equally "open" or "resonant." When you say the vowel sound in "aah" (like a doctor asking you to open your mouth), your mouth is wide open, air flows freely, and the sound is very resonant. When you say "p" or "t", you briefly block airflow entirely and then release it — these sounds are closed and abrupt, carrying very little resonance.

Linguists rank speech sounds on what's called a sonority scale (from highest to lowest):

  • Vowels (like a, e, i, o, u) → highest sonority. Most open, most resonant.
  • Glides (like w in "wet", y in "yet") → very high sonority.
  • Liquids (like l and r) → high sonority.
  • Nasals (like m, n, ng) → moderate sonority.
  • Fricatives (like f, v, s, z, sh) → lower sonority.
  • Stop consonants (like p, b, t, d, k, g) → lowest sonority. Most closed, most abrupt.

Why does this matter? Because sonority explains how syllables are built in human language.

There is a principle in linguistics called the Sonority Sequencing Principle. It states that within a syllable, sounds must rise in sonority toward the center (the vowel) and then fall in sonority toward the edges.

Take the word "plant":

  • p (very low sonority) → l (high sonority) → a (highest sonority) → n (moderate sonority) → t (very low sonority)

The sonority rises as you approach the vowel a, then falls as you move away from it. This creates the natural "shape" of a syllable.

This is why some sound combinations feel natural in a language and others don't. If you tried to start a word with lp- (as in lpin), you'd be starting with high sonority and then dropping — which violates the expected rise toward the vowel. It sounds wrong. English doesn't allow it. The sonority principle is part of the reason.

This sense of the word is entirely separate from the musical sense — it's not about richness or beauty. It's purely a measure of acoustic energy and openness in the vocal tract.

ContextWhat "sonority" means

Sonority as a noun has two main worlds:

In general and musical use: The rich, full, resonant, deep quality of sound. The property that makes a voice or instrument sound warm, powerful, and substantial — as opposed to thin, sharp, or flat. A word of admiration.

In linguistics: A technical measure of how open and acoustically resonant a speech sound is. Vowels have the most sonority; stop consonants the least. This scale governs the structure of syllables in human language.

Both meanings share the same root idea — sounds that are open, resonant, and carrying — but applied in very different ways.
